clinicalPearls: Acute gout classically presents as an abrupt, exquisitely painful monoarthritis, most often of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), with redness, swelling, and warmth peaking within hours
It is caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in and around joints on a background of chronic hyperuricaemia and urate supersaturation

Definitive diagnosis is by joint aspiration and polarised light microscopy showing needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, often seen within phagocytes during an attack
Serum urate can be normal or even low during an acute flare, so a normal value does not exclude gout; the level is best measured or repeated once the attack has settled
Common triggers and associations include alcohol, purine-rich food and fructose, diuretics, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome
Acute attacks are managed with anti-inflammatory therapy, choosing between a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, or a corticosteroid according to comorbidity

Urate-lowering therapy using a treat-to-target approach (lowering serum urate below the saturation threshold) is indicated for recurrent attacks, tophi, or urate arthropathy, with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis when it is introduced
Urate-lowering therapy should not be started or stopped during an acute attack, and any established urate-lowering therapy is continued through a flare rather than interrupted
reference.pathophysiology: Sustained hyperuricaemia, arising more often from renal under-excretion than from urate overproduction, leads to supersaturation of extracellular fluid and precipitation of monosodium urate crystals within joints and soft tissues. The crystals are engulfed by resident phagocytes and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, driving release of interleukin-1 beta and an intense neutrophil-rich inflammatory response that produces the acute attack. Repeated crystal deposition and low-grade chronic inflammation eventually generate tophi and cause structural joint damage.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis, which must be excluded and can coexist
additionalInvestigations: Joint aspiration with polarised microscopy for negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals and to exclude infection
Synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count
Serum urate, interpreted with the timing caveat and repeated once the attack settles
Renal function and assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity
Radiographs for chronic 'punched-out' erosions in longstanding disease
Dual-energy CT to detect and characterise urate deposits when the diagnosis is uncertain
Ultrasound for the 'double contour' sign of urate over articular cartilage
redFlags: Fever with a hot swollen joint that may represent septic arthritis rather than, or in addition to, gout
Rapid polyarticular presentation in a systemically unwell patient
Renal impairment or urolithiasis complicating management
A tophus with skin ulceration or secondary infection
reference.prognosis: Gout is highly treatable: with effective urate-lowering therapy to target, crystals dissolve, attacks cease, and tophi regress over time; poor adherence or untreated hyperuricaemia, however, leads to recurrent attacks, chronic arthropathy, and progressive joint destruction.
pitfalls: Excluding gout because the serum urate is normal during an acute attack
Starting or stopping urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare, which can prolong or precipitate attacks
Failing to exclude coexisting septic arthritis in a hot joint
Treating a target urate number without a structured treat-to-target strategy and prophylaxis at initiation
Overlooking associated cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic disease
